newsitem.title: USA: Talks continue to resolve GM truck strike.
newsitem.headline: Talks continue to resolve GM truck strike.

text.p: Talks aimed at resolving a five-day-old General Motors Corp full-size pickup truck plant strike continued Tuesday, but United Auto Workers union officials indicated progress was slow.
About 2,700 members of UAW Local 2209 walked off the job at the plant in Fort Wayne, Ind., after the two sides failed to reach agreement on contract terms by the strike deadline at 10 a.m. March 14.

The union wants GM to address health and safety issues and add more jobs to cut down on overtime. GM, which would like to shed about 30,000 hourly U.S. workers over the next three years through attrition, has thus far balked at the UAW's demands.
Company and union bargainers resumed talks about 8 a.m. EST Tuesday after working until 6 p.m. Monday, said GM spokesman Daniel Flores. He decined to characterize the discussions.
"Obviously we're encouraged that both sides are meeting and the talks are continuing," he said.

Although dealers have ample inventories of Chevrolet C/K and GMC Sierra pickup trucks, Burnham Securities Inc analyst David Healy said GM may decide to settle the dispute within a week or two before losing too much more production.

"I would think it's likely to be settled sooner rather than later," he said. "To me, it looks like one of those things the company could give a little bit on without setting a precedent for the other (locals) that are still hanging."
GM is still working to reach agreements with about 40 percent of its 105 UAW locals. Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp are both much closer to wrapping up all of their local agreements.
Last November, the Big Three automakers and the UAW reached a new national agreement that acts as a framework for settling local pacts.
The Fort Wayne discussions are being closely watched because it is the first local UAW situation to erupt in a strike since the national agreement was signed.

The Fort Wayne plant makes about 5,500 regular cab C/K and Sierra pickup trucks a week. Healy at Burnham Securities estimates GM would lose profits of about $25 million a week from the strike. However, he said the automaker could make up some of that production in the second quarter.
GM declined to comment on how much the strike is costing the automaker.
